Text1:
Scope notes are written for a reader who has never seen the box and never will unless the note
persuades them to ask for it. Two or three sentences are usually enough. Name the people, the
places and the kind of record; say what years are covered thickly and what years are thin; and
mention anything a searcher would be glad to know in advance, such as a gap, a fragile item, or a
bundle that is written in shorthand. Do not summarise the contents as though writing a history of
the town. the town.

Text1:
The reference number is the only thing that must never change. Titles can be corrected, date ranges
narrowed, scope notes rewritten, but the number printed on the box, written in the register and
quoted in a researcher's footnote has to point at the same material for as long as the archive exists.

Text1:
Every catalogue entry names the volunteer who wrote it and the month it was written. That is not a
matter of credit. When an entry turns out to be wrong, which happens, the quickest way to
understand the error is to ask the person who made it what they were looking at, and when a whole
run of entries shares a misunderstanding it helps to know they came from one hand in one season

Item-level listing, where every letter or photograph gets its own line, is done only for the collections
the committee has named. It multiplies the work by a factor of twenty or more and, for most boxes,
adds little that a good scope note does not already give. When an item-level list is made, it lives as a
